_note: Authored, not text-mined. Each edge is a structural relation that can be pointed to in the index: its 'why' is a verbatim quote from the entry of one of its two ends (gate check 80). Relations: 'rests on' (weight depends on), 'rests on rule' (rests on a reading rule or method premise), 'licenses' (opens the category), 'repairs' (fixes a weakness in), 'bounds' (limits how far it may be pushed), 'answers' (responds to an argument for the other view), 'supports' (adds weight to). If a premise is set aside: 'rests on' and 'rests on rule' fall if ANY target falls; 'licenses' falls only if ALL licensors fall; the others never carry a fall. Every id is validated against master.json at build time. An argument not traced to a premise is listed in open_questions with the question it raises, never given a guessed edge.

premises.name: Rule 1: grammatical-historical
premises.say: what the author meant his first readers to understand

premises.name: Rule 2: established usage
premises.say: a word means what the author's own repeated use of it means

premises.name: Rule 3: context
premises.say: the passage, the book and the canon decide the meaning

premises.name: Rule 4: Scripture interprets Scripture
premises.say: the letters help us read the narratives (WCF 1.9)

premises.name: Rule 5: good and necessary consequence
premises.say: a duty may be deduced, not only read off a command (WCF 1.6)

premises.name: The narrative rule (A2)
premises.say: a narrative binds only where Scripture commends it, commands it, repeats it, or grounds it

premises.name: Christ extends to later believers (A4)
premises.say: something passes from the Twelve to the church (John 17:20)

premises.name: Christ's example commanded (A5)
premises.say: Scripture commands conformity to Christ (1 Pet 2:21; 1 John 2:6); held fixed, never set aside here

premises.name: Jesus' training of the Twelve as a pattern for a congregation
premises.say: every argument the author tags as needing Jesus' example to bind; those that only partly need it stay standing, and each sheet says which

open_questions.q: C8's case draws on the daily meeting of Acts 2:46 (narrative), and its rejoinder says Heb 3:13, a precept, "survives untouched." Does C8 fall if the narrative rule (A2) is set aside, or does its Heb 3:13 half stand on rule 1?

C18 argues from how Jesus and the apostles formed people by prayer (narrative), and says its precept weight is carried by Acts 6:4 and Matt 9:38. Does it fall with the narrative rule (A2), or does the precept half stand on its own?

C4's case draws on the sending of the seventy-two (Luke 10, narrative), and its rejoinder rests reproduction on Acts 8:4 and 18:26 and on two letters (2 Tim 2:2; Titus 2:3–5). Does C4 fall if the narrative rule (A2) is set aside, or does its precept half stand on its own?
C2 argues from the confessional standards. Does it rest on one of the five reading rules, or should "our standards" be a premise of its own?
C9 reads baptism through WCF 27.2 and 28.1. A reading rule, or the standards as their own premise?
C16 reads BCO 8-3 closely. The five rules are for Scripture; is the Book of Church Order a premise of its own?
C17 counts the means of grace in WSC 88. Same question: the standards as a premise of their own?
C7 builds its definition of maturity from Col 1:28, Eph 4:13–16 and Heb 5:14. Rule 4 (Scripture interprets Scripture), or rule 1 read text by text?
D1 (disciple-making reserved to officers) reads the shepherd texts plainly. Which rule does it rest on, if any one more than the others?
D4 rests on C16 (our polity) and on Deut 6 and Eph 6:4 as commands. If C16 is answered by "the standards", is D4 traced through it, or does it need a rule of its own?
No entry names rule 5 (good and necessary consequence) in its own words; the index states it in A1 and A5. B1 and B2 draw duties from what Jesus did, which is that rule’s work. Do they rest on it?
